extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars of literature and Shakespeare
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic entry summarising A Midsummer Night's Dream: characters, plot, sources, themes, critical history, and stage/film adaptations. Aimed at readers seeking background, interpretation, and critical perspectives on the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of multiple plot lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's multiple interconnecting plots should form a coherent unity rather than appear disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schlegel perceived unity in the multiple plot lines and argued that connections (for example, Bottom's donkey head reflecting his nature and the burlesque Pyramus and Thisbe) indicate intentional structural cohesion rather than random incident. Critics who praise unity emphasise how themes and motifs interweave across subplots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry versus stage suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the play's poetry and lyricism suit theatrical performance or are better appreciated on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Hazlitt and others argued the play is 'better as a written work than a staged production' and that stage productions can reduce it to a 'dull pantomime'. Critics weigh the quality of verse, lyricism, and poetic language against practical demands of staging and performance history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of the supernatural/fairies
rubrics_metrics.description: How credibly and effectively the play depicts fairies and supernatural elements within a theatrical or poetic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Dryden defended inclusion of fairies as permissible poetic invention when derived from 'popular belief'; critics consider whether supernatural depiction is artistically justified and integrated into the play's conventions and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum and social stratification (class appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the treatment and prominence of lower-class characters (the mechanicals) violates classical decorum by overshadowing aristocratic characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edmond Malone criticised a 'lack of proper decorum'—the lower-class characters play larger roles than their social betters. Evaluations consider period expectations about social hierarchy on stage and whether subversion of hierarchy is a flaw or a deliberate comic strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and plot quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived originality, maturity, and plausibility of the play's plot and its mix of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Francis Gentleman called the plot 'puerile' and an 'odd mixture of incidents'; others praise its imaginative combinations. Critics judge whether plot elements cohere aesthetically or feel forced/immature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation and individuality (especially the mechanicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vividness, distinctiveness, and dramatic function of the characters, notably Bottom and the group of artisans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Cowden Clarke and Elizabeth Sewell emphasise the mechanicals' individualisation and richness; Bottom is variously read as conceited but imaginative or as a representative of human nature. Evaluations focus on comic effectiveness, empathy, and how well characters serve themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal consistency (problems with time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency and plausibility of the play's temporal references (e.g., moon phases, timing of scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note apparent contradictions—Theseus' remark about 'four happy days' vs moonless wood-night and rehearsal in moonlight—leading to debate about whether such ambiguities are errors or purposeful liminality (a 'dark of the moon' period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreamlike quality / interpretation as a dream
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the play functions as a dream (structurally or thematically) and if that reading explains its tone and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Taylor Coleridge argued the entire play should be seen as a dream, which explains its light characterisation and fantastical events. Critics use this criterion to justify incongruities and to interpret tone and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of love (themes of lovers' bliss and darker aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the play represents love: its blissful, carnivalesque side as well as its darker, irrational, or destructive tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Bevington argued the play shows the 'dark side of love'—fairy mischief trivialises love and exposes its caprices. Critics assess whether treatment of love is comic, satiric, tragic, or ambivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnivalesque / festivity and inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the play embodies carnivalesque features (Bacchanalia, Saturnalia), festive inversion of norms, and social release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Wiles and Harold Bloom endorse readings of the play as aristocratic carnival literature written for wedding celebrations; critics examine how carnivalistic inversion informs character behaviour and thematic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous sexuality and queer readings
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's openness to interpretations of non-normative or ambiguous sexualities and homoerotic significations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglas E. Green explores 'homoerotic significations' and 'queer' disruptions in the text; critics consider textual moments (Oberon's obsession, Titania/Bottom episode, lovers' confusions) for alternative-sexuality readings while placing them in historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender roles and patriarchal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: How gender relations, male dominance, marriage, and transfer of authority over women are depicted and critiqued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Louis Montrose and Leonard Tennenhouse discuss male dominance, the law requiring daughters to obey fathers, and how carnival moments break down male power. Critics assess whether the play endorses, critiques, or ambivalently presents patriarchal structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sources and intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation to earlier texts and myths (Ovid, Chaucer, Aristophanes, medieval poems) and how source-material shapes originality and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars trace inspirations—Ovid's Metamorphoses, Chaucer's 'The Knight's Tale', Aristophanes' Birds, Der Busant—and judge the play by how imaginatively it adapts and transforms these antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for performance and adaptation history
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the play adapts to different staging, film, opera, ballet, and other media, and the quality of specific productions or adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note performance history and adaptations (e.g., many film and stage versions). Some judge the play's success by its staging record and how directors realize its fantastical elements; others note that early adaptations altered the text significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism and imagery (flowers, blood, sexual symbolism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of recurring symbols (love-in-idleness, flowers, blood) and their sexual, menstrual, or erotic significations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montrose links Oberon's juice to menstrual blood and sexual blood of virgins; critics evaluate how symbolic imagery contributes to readings of sexuality, desire, and power in the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and unconscious readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether elements of the play are best read as manifestations of unconscious drives, erotic imagination, or psychological symbolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georg Brandes and others suggest Oberon's magic typifies the 'sorcery of the erotic imagination' and the play looks inward to the unconscious. This approach gauges depth of psychological resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical or allegorical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading the play as an allegory or ethical construct about sensual love, morality, and social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gervinus argued the play is an allegorical depiction of the errors of sensual love and reads characters and incidents as moral types; critics using this criterion assess moral messaging and allegorical consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy, burlesque, and metatheatrical playfulness (Pyramus and Thisbe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of the play's comic devices, burlesque elements, and the play-within-a-play as parody or metatheatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanicals' performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' is read as burlesque and parody of contemporary dramatic topos; critics judge comic timing, metatheatrical commentary, and whether the device enhances thematic depth or merely provides low comedy.
